brief.head: Stone Age hardware
brief.text: Modern humans have had only about 4,000 generations, Ajay Shah said, too few to change the brain’s hardware. Many fallacies are instincts that once worked and now misfire. {045-C01}

brief.head: Three ways to disagree
brief.text: We fight over facts, over values or over how we reason, Shah said. He hopes logic, argument and proof can be common ground. {045-C02}

brief.head: A gift that grows
brief.text: Newton, the Magna Carta and the transistor were each made in some corner of the world, and everyone came out better off. {045-C04}

brief.head: Varma’s Law
brief.text: Amit Varma, being “a little vain”, named a law after himself: most interference in free markets redistributes from the poor to the rich. {045-C05}

brief.head: Not a company
brief.text: A country is not a firm, Shah said: a state’s every move ripples through the whole economy, and it wields coercion. {045-C08}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on why we keep fighting
lead.head: Five traps for Stone Age brains
body: The two hosts could not agree on who should speak first. Amit Varma turned the fumble into the question of the hour: why do we keep fighting? {045-J01}

Their answer, over the next 55 minutes, was that our brains are wired for a world that no longer exists. The world is too complex to grasp, so we make sense of it through simple stories. Those stories clash with one another, and sometimes all of them clash with reality.
“From a hundred thousand years ago to today, the period of modern man is a mere 4,000 generations,” Ajay Shah said, “which is not enough to materially move the needle on our hardware.” {045-C01}

Taking their framework from Thomas Sowell’s *Economic Facts and Fallacies*, the hosts walked through five fallacies that grow out of instincts formed in small tribes of hunter-gatherers. Each once served the tribe well. Each misfires in a modern economy. {045-R01}
## The five traps
The zero-sum fallacy treats the economy as a fixed pie, so that one person’s gain must be another’s loss. {045-C03}
The fallacy of composition assumes that what is true of a part is true of the whole. {045-C06}
The post-hoc fallacy decides that because one thing followed another, the first must have caused the second. {045-C09}
The chess-pieces fallacy imagines society as a board that a planner can arrange. {045-C12}
The open-ended fallacy forgets that resources are limited and have other uses. {045-C13}
The examples ran from a college hostel in Pune to the banks of the Nile and a monkey throwing darts.
## Why it matters

For the hosts the stakes are practical. Zero-sum thinking, Varma argued, drives statism and the confusion of inequality with poverty. Since 1991, hundreds of millions of Indians have left poverty even as inequality rose.
“In a world of double thank you moments,” Varma said, “the only way that I can profit is by making you better off.” {045-C03}

The fallacy of composition, Shah said, is the core difference between thinking like a firm and thinking about an economy. What makes sense for one exporter, or one tomato farmer, can wreck things when everyone does it, and worse when the state uses its power to make everyone do it. {045-C06}

Millions of Indians, Varma said, stayed poor for longer than they should have, because planners did not trust people’s ingenuity. Shah was less sure that the lesson had been learnt. “Gentle readers,” he said, “see how optimistic Amit is.” {045-J11}
## How to stop fighting

Knowing these fallacies is easy, Shah warned; internalising them takes a long time. In a doctor, engineer and MBA India that treats knowledge as a trade to be applied, he said, “there is a great crisis of thinking”. {045-C18}

Both hosts ended with books about the fighting itself. Shah recommended Christopher Blattman’s *Why We Fight*, glad that an economist had “opened the box of violence”. {045-R24} Varma chose Arnold Kling’s *The Three Languages of Politics*, which argues that political tribes talk past each other because they start from different core values: equality, tradition or freedom. {045-R25}
Recognising the other person’s first principle, Varma said, is also a way of recognising their humanity. {045-C17}
And if the fighting never quite stops? Varma reached for an old motto: “Pessimism of the intellect, optimism of the will.” {045-J18}

second.label: The Great Depression
second.head: The crash didn’t do it
second.deck: Amit Varma, drawing on Thomas Sowell, blames what came after 1929
body: The standard story is that the stock market crash of 1929 caused the Great Depression. Amit Varma, drawing on Thomas Sowell, told a different one. {045-S04}

In the months after the crash, unemployment peaked at about 9 per cent, and by June 1930 it was down to around 6.5 per cent. {#unemployment} Then the government began to intervene, first with the Smoot-Hawley tariff and then with a series of other measures. That is when things exploded.

Sowell also points to a later stock market crash that was followed by decades of strong growth. Varma added that Amity Shlaes’s *The Forgotten Man*, if he remembered correctly, makes a similar case. {045-R10}

quote.text: It wasn’t the stock market crash. It was a whole bunch of interventions which led to the problem.

second.caption: the Great Depression

third.head: Nile floods, coat blamed
body: A witch doctor claims that every spring he takes off his coat, and then the Nile floods, so the river must be answering his coat. The sequence is real, Ajay Shah said. The causal claim is absurd. {045-S02}
Press a button and get a biscuit a second later, and two or three tries will convince you that you caused it. Make it ten hours, and the mind can no longer connect the two. {045-C10}
Our sense of cause and effect, Shah argued, was built for a world of tigers and deer, where effects follow causes quickly. So we must lean on evidence and data rather than gut feel.
Amit Varma, who is on a keto diet, did not want the biscuit at all. “Bacon strips,” he said, “another matter.” {045-J06}
third.caption: the witch doctor’s coat

p2.title: The five fallacies
p2.deck: From Thomas Sowell’s *Economic Facts and Fallacies*, as argued over by Amit Varma and Ajay Shah

sections.label: Fallacy One
sections.head: Thank you. No, thank you
sections.caption: the zero-sum fallacy
body: When a tribe splits a deer, every chunk one hunter takes is a chunk another cannot have. Our instincts were formed in that world, Amit Varma said, which is why we so readily see the economy as a fixed pie. {045-C03}

Modern exchange is different. When you buy a coffee, you say thank you and the seller says thank you, because both of you are better off. Varma took the image from the columnist John Stossel, who calls it the double thank-you moment. {045-R02}

Treat the world as a fixed pie and redistribution looks like the answer. But redistribution always trades off against growth, Varma said, and what a poor country needs is growth. Since 1991, hundreds of millions of Indians have left poverty even as inequality rose.
## The greatest positive-sum game

Ajay Shah took the argument further. Newton, the Magna Carta and the transistor were each created in some corner of the world, and everyone came out better off: the inventors of the transistor did not gain at our expense. Knowledge, he said, is “the greatest positive sum game story of the world”. {045-C04}

In personal life, Varma argued against crabby scarcity thinking and for generosity, because someone else’s success is not your loss. Shah’s book for the occasion was Robert Axelrod’s *The Evolution of Cooperation*, which works out the best response to being wronged: strike back once, but not twice, not thrice, not forever. {045-R06}

quote.text: In a world of double thank you moments, the only way that I can profit is by making you better off.

sections.label: Fallacy Two
sections.head: When everyone stands up
sections.caption: the fallacy of composition
body: Amit Varma read out Thomas Sowell’s illustration: “A baseball fan at a ballpark can see the game better by standing up. But if all the fans stand up, they will not all see better.” {045-C06}

This is the fallacy of composition, the belief that what is true of a part is true of the whole. Politicians help one group and present its gains as gains for society, which is really robbing Peter to pay Paul.

Ajay Shah sees it as the core difference between thinking like a firm and thinking about an economy. Exporting more makes sense for one company. Using state power to subsidise land, electricity or the exchange rate so that every company exports can unbalance the economy. The test, he said, is always the same: what if everyone does it?
## The flip side

Varma turned the fallacy inside out. Stereotyping takes a trait seen in one member of a group and paints every member with it. One sociopathic economist does not make all economists sociopaths, he said, assuring Shah that he was not one of them. {045-J07}
People regress to the mean, he said: neither angels nor demons. He read out a line from Tim Urban to the same effect: “Angels and demons aren’t real.” {045-R07}

quote.text: We are all human, we are all frail, and we are all beautiful.

sections.label: Fallacy Three
sections.head: Wet streets don’t cause rain
sections.caption: the post-hoc fallacy
body: Something happened, and then something else happened, so the first thing must have caused the second. That, Amit Varma said, is the post-hoc fallacy: *post hoc ergo propter hoc*. {045-C09}

Its cousin, *cum hoc ergo propter hoc*, assumes that two things happening together must be causally linked. And Michael Crichton’s phrase, “wet streets cause rain”, captures the arrow pointing the wrong way. {045-R09}

These shortcuts made sense in a simple world, where a rustle in the bush meant a tiger. Varma argued that religion and ritual grew out of such simple causal stories, for example about what brings rain. In a complex world they mislead us constantly, especially in economics.
## A short-range radar

Ajay Shah offered a thought experiment. Press a button and get a biscuit one second later, and you see the cause at once. Make the delay ten hours and you are lost. “The human mind is congenitally unable to see cause and effect playing out across longer timescales,” he said. {045-C10}

The personal lesson, for Varma, was humility about the stories we tell about ourselves. Shah’s version for firms: compare your results with simply holding your industry’s shares. Only the outperformance is yours. {045-C11}

quote.text: 98% of what happens to each of us is sheer dumb luck.

sections.label: Fallacy Four
sections.head: People are not pawns
sections.caption: the chess-pieces fallacy
body: Adam Smith warned of the “man of system”, who imagines he can arrange the members of a great society as easily as a hand arranges the pieces on a chessboard. Friedrich Hayek called the same belief the fatal conceit. {045-R12}

Top-down control works for a tribe, or a family firm of ten people, Amit Varma said. At scale, nobody has the information. Order emerges instead through “human action, but not human design”, in Adam Ferguson’s phrase. {045-J15}

Ajay Shah traced the idea “all the way to selfish gene”: every organism optimises for itself, so nobody can suppress each person’s drive to pursue their own life. He could not resist recommending a Leonard Cohen poem in which a slave says that any system you design without us will not work. {045-R18}
For individuals, Varma said, the lesson is to focus on processes and habits, not grand goals.

quote.text: The truth is we are not pieces on a chessboard that you can make things go the way they want.

sections.label: Fallacy Five
sections.head: There is no free lunch
sections.caption: the open-ended fallacy
body: Health, safety and open space are open-ended desires. Who could be against them? But resources are limited and have other uses, Amit Varma said, quoting Thomas Sowell. {045-C13}
India’s biggest religion, he said, is government. We assume that *mai-baap sarkar*, the parent-government, will pay for everything, as if money were unlimited and cost nothing. {045-J14}

Ajay Shah invoked Milton Friedman: there is no free lunch. Every government rupee is extracted through taxation, which is coercive and costly. A responsible policy thinker, he said, should pair every proposal for more spending with matching cuts elsewhere. {045-J16}
## The expert’s test

Shah offered a contrarian test of expertise in health. The Indian government spends poorly, and prevention is better than cure, so the sophisticated expert asks for less government spending on healthcare, and more on public health. {045-C14}

Coercion is worse than spending, he argued, because it has no budget. “In spending, there is a budget constraint,” he said. “But unfortunately, when it gets to coercion, coercion can be limitless.” {045-C15}
## Your own open-ended fallacy

For Varma, with age, the binding constraint has shifted from money to time. He cited Steve Jobs’s advice to his designer Jonathan Ive: learn to say no to things that you love. This is not a productivity fetish, he added. Time to relax and chill out is useful too. {045-C16}

quote.text: Many desirable things are advocated without regard to the most fundamental fact of economics, that resources are inherently limited and have alternative uses.
quote.who: Thomas Sowell, as read by Amit Varma

side.boxText: *Economic Facts and Fallacies* names fallacies that are foundational, in that many other errors grow out of them. Sowell is one of Amit Varma’s intellectual heroes, “still going strong at ninety plus”. {045-R01}

contQuote.text: One way to get past the fighting that we do, this ideological bickering that has become so common, is to recognize the other person’s core first principle, which is also to recognize that other person’s humanity.

stories.start: So my third I need to tell you a story
stories.end: So Ryan uh masturbated and then he got a big body
stories.caption: Amit Varma tells Ryan’s story
stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s college story, and a fallacy told for laughs
stories.head: The penance that built a Greek god
body: In the late 1980s and early 1990s, Amit Varma was a student at Ferguson College in Pune, so thin you could count the bones on his ribs. Fresh from a boys’ school, in an arts class that was about 80 per cent girls, he chose between the canteen and the tapri by the direction of the wind, so that his shirt would not blow against his ribs. Gyms were not yet part of the culture.
His consolation was Ryan, a devout Christian who was just as thin. If the two of them passed a group of girls who giggled, Varma could at least hope the giggling was at Ryan.
Then one day, through the open door of Ryan’s hostel room, Varma saw a horrifying sight. Ryan was doing push-ups. Thin boys whose bones are visible, Varma explained, do not do push-ups. {045-J03}
Ryan explained. Masturbation was a sin, and he had set himself 25 push-ups as the penance for each time. {#pushups} Varma, in his mind, did *sashtang pranam* and left.
Six months later Ryan was buff. The girls now giggled “at the improbable presence of a Greek god in their midst”, and Varma was the only one left whose bones were visible. {045-J04}
Then another friend from the hostel, whom Varma calls Varun, quietly asked how to get a body like Ryan’s. Varma told him, deliberately and as a joke: you have to masturbate.
“The lesson here,” Varma said, “is that deliberately out of a sense of humor, I committed a fallacy called the post hoc ergo propter hoc.” {045-S01}
stories.why: One thing happened, then another, so the first must have caused the second. The joke works because the real cause, the push-ups, was hidden inside the sequence. Many of our causal stories leave out the hidden middle step in the same way.
stories.postscript: Varma, now on keto and one meal a day, says he wants to be like Ryan. Which Ryan? “Any of the two.” {045-J06}

stories.caption: the dart-throwing monkey
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on luck, Infosys and the CEO
stories.head: The monkey beats the market
body: In finance, it is well accepted that a monkey throwing darts builds a decent portfolio, and that nearly all the clever humans picking stocks underperform it. Hope, though, springs eternal. “We each of us think that I’m in that 0.01% of the cool people that know what to do,” Ajay Shah said. {045-J10}
Nobody could have predicted the software boom from the mid-1990s. When Infosys went public in 1994, its IPO was mostly undersubscribed. {#ipo}

People inside a booming industry then credit their success to their own decisions. Shah’s honest test: how would you have done if you had simply bought shares in ten companies in your industry and done nothing? Only the outperformance over that baseline is yours.
“The world, the society attributes all firm success to the CEO,” he said, “and I think that is wrong.” {045-S06}
stories.why: Much of what passes for success is the luck of being in software rather than seafood. Separate the tailwind from your own contribution before crediting the CEO, or yourself.

stories.start: The fallacy of composition is all over economics
stories.end: use state coercion to force many people to behave like that
stories.caption: the tomato glut
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the fallacy of composition
stories.head: Too many tomatoes spoil the price
body: When tomatoes are scarce, a farmer reasons that he should plant tomatoes, spend lavishly on inputs and make a killing. For one farmer, that is sensible. {045-S05}
But a million farmers respond to the same prices. The market floods, the price falls to zero, and angry farmers pour truckloads of tomatoes on the roadside because they are not worth transporting.

Ajay Shah sees the same pattern in semiconductors. After the chip shortage, he said, “every idiot in the world” decided to build a fab, and he predicted a glut, and bankruptcies among chipmakers, within a year or two.
The disciplined question, he said, is always the same: what happens if everybody does this?

quote.text: What may be true for me in the small doesn’t work when a million people think the same.

stories.start: there's a great metaphor that expresses just this complexity
stories.caption: the swimming pool
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on why causes are hard to see
stories.head: Signal lost in the deep end
body: Does dropping a coin into water raise the level? In a laboratory, with a beaker and everything controlled, the experiment is easy. {045-S03}

“Now imagine you are doing this in a crowded swimming pool,” Amit Varma said. “It’s a big swimming pool, it is incredibly crowded, people are splashing around in it, it is windy and it is raining at the same time.” The data, he said, will mostly be garbage.
He had the metaphor from his friend Shruti Rajagopalan, who, he thinks, may have been quoting Don Boudreaux.

This is why economists love the post-war splits of North and South Korea and East and West Germany: they come close to a controlled experiment on free markets. “Spoiler alert,” Varma said: free markets won.
stories.why: Social science happens in the swimming pool, not the beaker. Real controlled experiments are rare, and confirmation bias fills the gap, so claims that X caused Y deserve humility.

quiz.q: Spring comes, the witch doctor takes off his coat, the Nile floods. Which fallacy says the coat did it?
quiz.a: Post hoc ergo propter hoc: after this, therefore because of this.

quiz.a: The fallacy of composition: what is true of a part is not true of the whole.

quiz.q: How many generations has modern man had, by Ajay Shah’s count, and why does it matter?

quiz.q: Whose phrase is “no free lunch”, and what did Shah use it for?
quiz.a: Milton Friedman’s. Government money is neither free nor infinite: every rupee has another use.

quiz.q: What should a sophisticated health expert in India ask for, according to Shah?
quiz.a: Less government spending on healthcare, and more on public health: prevention over cure.
